To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the structure of the actin-mysoin-ATP complex is indistinguishable in rapid freeze-fracture electron microscopy from that of rigor complexes, (2) the configuration of the myosm head is similar in the presence and absence of ATP, and (3) the myosin-actin cross-links used in previous studies are probably not in the rigor state in the presence of nucleotide.

the weakly bound complexes of myosins with ATP and ADP-Pi are similar to the rigor state, and the transition from the weakly bound to the strongly bound complexes does not involve a change in the angle of attachment of myosin to actin filament or in the configuration of most parts of the myosins.

the weakly bound complexes of myosins with actin filament in the presence of nucleotides are not different from those of the rigor complexes.

the weakly bound complexes of myosins-ATP and -ADP with actin are similar in their attachment to the actin helix and that the myosin subfragments-1 heads are not rigidly attached to the actin subfilament but can rotate freely.
the weakly bound myosin heads in these preparations do not tilt significantly in the absence of ATP, and the high affinity heads do not tilt significantly during ATP hydrolysis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the weakly bound myosin heads in the ATPase intermediate complexes are not in a position to interact directly with actin filamnets and therefore cannot be responsible for the force generation in muscle contraction.
the myosin and the actin filament are in the rigor state at all stages of the ATPase cycle.
the myosin-ATP complex is in the weakly bound state and the transition from weakly bound to high affinity state involves a conformational change in the actomyo-S1 complex.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the myosin-actin interaction is very similar at all stages of the ATPase cycle.
we were able to directly observe the intermediates in the myosin-actin ATPase cycle by rapid freezing and electron microscopy.
